newsitem.title: USA: Mubarak says violence may start if Israel persists. [CORRECTED 22:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Mubarak says violence may start if Israel persists. [CORRECTED 22:05 GMT]

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said Israel's hardline policy was forcing Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat into such a corner that "violence may start" against Israel and its allies.
"If Arafat disappears, the Palestinians will not sit with folded arms," Mubarak said in an interview with Time magazine to be published on Monday.
"Violence may start. Not only against the Israelis, but against those who support the Israelis."

Mubarak said he was "very, very, very upset" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he accused of derailing peace efforts by reneging on agreements to pull the Israeli army out of the West Bank town of Hebron.
"I heard that he wants to change the whole agreement on Hebron. But Arafat will be unable to do this. It will mean the failure of Arafat among his people," Mubarak said.

Mubarak, who declined an invitation to a recent Middle East summit at the White House, said Netanyahu's policies had also led to "strained" relations with Egypt, the first Arab country to negotiate with the Jewish state.
"The people are furious. Some elements in this country are saying 'Cut diplomatic relations.' I am very keen for the process to move forward, not to freeze diplomatic relations," he said.

Mubarak, who has refused to meet Netanyahu, has invited Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres to meet him in Egypt next week and will meet Israeli President Ezer Weizman, whose job is largely ceremonial, in Egypt on Monday.
The Egyptian leader said Israel will face a hostile audience at the Middle East economic summit in Cairo next month (corrects from "next week"), and that trade could suffer.
"If Mr. Netanyahu moves forward and respects his words, it would be helpful," Mubarak said. "They have lots of trade in the Arab world. If we don't reach a definite peace, all this trade will stop."
Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation held formal negotiations last week and were due to resume talks this week in Taba, Egypt.
